lessons.title: Case Study: India's Post-Covid Policy Mix (2020-2023)

body.text: The best way to learn how fiscal and monetary policy interact is to watch it actually happen. India's post-Covid journey runs through nearly every regime this course has covered: counter-cyclical alignment, an external shock nobody controlled, a hiking cycle, a fiscal tool deployed to fight inflation directly, and a slow handoff back toward complementary alignment.

body.title: India's fiscal deficit and repo rate, FY20-FY26 (illustrative)

body.text: Watch the two lines cross paths on this chart. They move together through the Covid shock (both falling or staying low), then diverge sharply through 2022 as monetary policy tightens while fiscal consolidation is still gradual, and slowly converge again by FY25-FY26. That shape is the entire policy mix framework from Chapter 1, playing out in one real, continuous episode.

markDefs.definition: Targeted Long Term Repo Operations: a Covid-era RBI facility that lent banks funds at the repo rate for up to three years, on condition the money was deployed into specific stressed sectors, corporate bonds and commercial paper, combining a liquidity tool with targeted credit support.

children.text: The nationwide lockdown in March 2020 produced the sharpest quarterly GDP contraction in India's independent history. The policy response was, correctly, maximal alignment: the government rolled out the Atmanirbhar Bharat packages, a mix of direct fiscal support, credit guarantees for small businesses, and food security measures, while the RBI cut the repo rate to 4.00%, its lowest level on record at the time, and deployed tools like
Targeted Long Term Repo Operations, or TLTRO

, alongside a loan moratorium and regulatory forbearance for stressed borrowers. This was textbook loose-loose counter-cyclical alignment from Chapter 3's earlier lesson, and it was the correct call given the scale of spare capacity the shock created.

body.label: FY21 real GDP growth (approx.)
body.context: India's sharpest full-year GDP contraction on record, the scale of demand collapse that justified maximal counter-cyclical alignment. Illustrative; check the latest National Accounts revision for the exact figure.

children.text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 sent global crude oil and commodity prices sharply higher. For an economy that imports the large majority of its crude oil needs, this was a direct, imported cost-push shock, not a domestic demand problem, and CPI inflation pushed above the RBI's upper tolerance band of 6% within months. The response that followed is worth studying closely, because it used both levers, not just one.

On the monetary side, the RBI delivered an off-cycle rate hike in May 2022, outside its scheduled bi-monthly calendar, signalling the urgency of the inflation problem, followed by a rapid sequence of further hikes through the rest of 2022. On the fiscal side, the government cut excise duty on petrol and diesel in May 2022, a direct fiscal tool aimed at lowering a specific, heavily weighted component of the inflation basket, rather than the demand-management fiscal tools covered in Chapter 2.

body.title: Is a Duty Cut Fiscal Loosening?
body.scenario: In May 2022, alongside its excise duty cut on fuel, the government's near-term revenue collection fell (duty foregone), which on paper widens the fiscal deficit relative to what it would otherwise have been. At the same time, this same move was explicitly aimed at lowering measured inflation, the same objective the RBI's rate hikes were pursuing.
body.prompt: Does this duty cut count as fiscal policy working against monetary policy (loosening while the RBI tightens) or as fiscal policy supporting monetary policy's inflation fight? Explain the distinction.
body.modelAnswer: It is fiscal loosening in a narrow accounting sense, revenue was foregone and the deficit widened relative to the counterfactual. But it is not demand-side fiscal loosening of the kind covered in Chapter 2, it did not add purchasing power or aggregate demand into the economy. It directly lowered a specific price the CPI basket measures, working through the same inflation objective the RBI's hikes were pursuing, just through a different transmission channel (direct price levels rather than demand and credit conditions). This is a useful reminder that classifying a fiscal move as loose or tight requires asking what it actually does to demand and prices, not just what it does to the deficit number on paper.

children.text: Phase 3: Fiscal Consolidation Resumes While Monetary Policy Holds Tight (2022-2024)

Once the acute Covid emergency passed, fiscal policy pivoted back toward consolidation, deficit reduction resumed as a stated multi-year glide path, with the spending mix increasingly weighted toward capex over broad-based welfare support, the capex-versus-consumption distinction from Chapter 2. The RBI, having taken the repo rate to 6.50% by February 2023, held it there for an extended stretch, roughly two years, unwilling to cut until it was convinced inflation had durably settled back toward target rather than just dipped temporarily.

columns.label: Fiscal policy
points: Deficit consolidation resumed as a stated glide path
Spending mix tilted toward capex over broad welfare spending
One targeted exception: the May 2022 duty cut, aimed at inflation, not demand

columns.label: Monetary policy
points: Rapid hiking cycle through 2022 to 6.50% by February 2023
Extended hold at 6.50% for roughly two years
Stance kept at withdrawal of accommodation well after the last hike, signalling no rush to ease

children.text: By the time inflation had cooled durably enough for the RBI's comfort, fiscal consolidation was already well underway, deficit heading toward the 4.4% of GDP FY26 target from Lesson 1. That combination, a government that had already done the consolidating, meeting a central bank now confident enough to ease, is precisely the complementary handoff alignment described earlier in this chapter. The RBI's first cut came in February 2025, with further cuts through the year taking the repo rate to roughly 5.50%.

body.title: India's post-Covid policy mix, key milestones

events.title: Lockdown and emergency rate cut
events.description: Nationwide lockdown begins; RBI cuts the repo rate sharply toward its eventual 4.00% floor, alongside a loan moratorium and regulatory forbearance.

events.title: Atmanirbhar Bharat and TLTRO
events.description: Multiple rounds of fiscal support packages roll out alongside continued RBI liquidity support, including TLTRO, sustaining the loose-loose counter-cyclical alignment.

events.title: Russia-Ukraine war begins
events.description: Global crude oil and commodity prices spike, an imported cost-push shock that pushes CPI inflation above the RBI's tolerance band.

events.title: Off-cycle hike and excise duty cut
events.description: RBI delivers an unscheduled inter-meeting rate hike; government cuts excise duty on petrol and diesel, a fiscal tool aimed directly at the inflation print.

events.title: Repo rate reaches 6.50%
events.description: The hiking cycle concludes; the RBI holds at this level for an extended stretch while fiscal consolidation resumes.

events.title: The handoff begins
events.description: RBI delivers its first rate cut of the cycle as inflation cools durably, alongside continued fiscal consolidation, the complementary alignment pattern from this chapter.

body.title: Naming the Phase
body.question: Which phase of this case study represents the clearest example of tight monetary policy combined with fiscal policy that had not yet fully pivoted to consolidation?
options: Phase 2 (early 2022): the global shock and the immediate policy reaction
Phase 3 (2022-2024): the extended hold at 6.50% while consolidation was still a multi-year glide path in progress, not yet complete
body.explanation: Phase 1 was loose-loose alignment. Phase 2 was the shock itself and the initial reaction, using both levers together against inflation. Phase 4 is the completed handoff, tight fiscal plus loose monetary, both levers now aligned. Phase 3 is the transitional stretch where monetary policy was fully tight (holding at 6.50%) while fiscal consolidation was still a multi-year process working toward its target, the period of least alignment between the two levers in this entire case study.

body.title: Building Your Own Case-Study Timeline for Any Economy
steps: Plot the fiscal deficit and the policy rate on the same timeline, exactly as the chart in this lesson does, to see convergence and divergence visually
Identify the shock or turning point that changed the picture, in India's case, the Covid lockdown and later the Russia-Ukraine war
Check whether fiscal tools used during a crisis are demand-side (adding purchasing power) or direct price-level tools (like duty cuts), since they work through different channels
Note how long monetary policy holds at an extreme once fiscal policy has already reversed direction, since that gap is where policy mix friction tends to concentrate
Identify the handoff point, if one exists, where a completed fiscal consolidation and a confident monetary easing cycle actually meet

body.text: Nothing in this lesson is investment advice. It is an educational case study of how fiscal and monetary policy interacted through a specific historical period, consistent with SEBI's guidelines for registered research analysts on this platform.

points: India's post-Covid journey moved through nearly every regime this course covers: loose-loose alignment, an external shock, a hiking cycle, and a complementary handoff
The May 2022 excise duty cut is a useful reminder that a fiscal move can widen the deficit on paper while still supporting, not undermining, the monetary policy objective
The 2022-2024 stretch, tight monetary policy held firm while fiscal consolidation was still a multi-year glide path in progress, was the period of least alignment in this entire episode
The 2025 handoff, RBI easing once fiscal consolidation was already well underway, is the complementary alignment pattern from earlier in this chapter, playing out in real time
Plotting the fiscal deficit and policy rate on one timeline is a transferable technique for reading any economy's policy mix history, not just India's
